messages.author: e19ea506112fd25b
messages.subject: mixed-effects model in stan
parts:
Hi,

Can anybody explain why there are convergence problems in mixed-effect model while the nlme counterpart provides a reasonable R2=89%?

The stan model is attached. It doesn't converge as well as gives multiple:
Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
Error in function stan::prob::normal_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Location parameter is 1.#QNAN:0, but must be finite!
If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.

Thanks a lot for suggestions,
Linas

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] mixed-effects model in stan
parts:
What is nlme and are you sure you're fitting the same model?

With this kind of model, your problem is most likely identifiability.
You can often diagnose this empirically by plotting correlations of
parameters.

I think your problem may be here:

// priors
for (i in 1 : 4)
beta [i] ~ normal (beta0 [i], 0.1 * beta0 [i]);

This isn't identified in itself because beta and beta0 are variables
and you only have a single observation. But then I see
that you're using beta elsewhere, but it could still be a problem.


There are a lot of things you can do for efficiency
and numerical stability, too.

Most importantly, use a Cholesky-based parameterization
for Omega rather than decomposing it. There's an extended
example in the priors section of the regression chapter in
the Stan 2.5 manual.

Then use a non-centered parameterization for hierarchical
priors --- there's also a discussion in the manual in the
chapter on reparameterizations.

You can pass vectors directly to increment_log_prob now,
so you don't need the sum() in sum(log_lik).

We have quad forms with diagonals, so you don't need to
create diagonal matrices and multiply.

You can replace

for (i in 1 : 4) mu_prior [i] <- 0;

with

mu_prior <- rep_vector(0.0, 4);

not that it's an issue in your code being in the transformed
data block.

Use local variables in the transformed parameters block so
things don't get saved, like D, L and DL (though you really want
to completely replace those using the direct Cholesky parameterization).

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] mixed-effects model in stan
parts:
Using

real<lower=0> x;

implicitly works on the log(x) scale and then applies exp() to
get back to positive. That is, Stan treats x_raw as (-inf,inf) and
defines x <- exp(x_raw). This also applies a Jacobian, allowing
you to define a sampling distribution for x, e.g.,

x ~ lognormal(0,5);

If you explicitly define:

real x;

with sampling distribution

x ~ normal(1,5);

the computation is a bit different because we don't need to
apply the Jacobian to and from the lognormal. So maybe it's more
arithmetically stable.

- Bob
